Mint.name: Mint
Mint.origin: Europe and western Asia; cultivated worldwide
Mint.description: This profile means spearmint (Mentha spicata), with a sweet, green, gently cooling aroma and less menthol-driven sharpness than peppermint. Use fresh leaves for lift in sauces, salads, legumes, tea, and grilled meats.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1/4-1 cup fresh leaves per 4 servings, depending on dish
1/2-1 cup leaves per 4 servings, served fresh

top_pairings.note: Citrusy seed warmth gives spearmint a rounded base in chutneys and dressings.
Earthy cumin balances mint's cool, sweet lift in yogurt sauces and legumes.
A dry peppery finish reins in mint's sweetness.
Tart, berry-like acidity sharpens the fresh herbal character.
Soft sweet warmth links mint with fruit, rice, and braised dishes.
Ginger's bright heat adds depth to mint's clean cooling impression.

substitutes.notes: This profile specifically represents spearmint; use it as the direct identity.
More mentholated and sharper; use less, especially in savory dishes.
Can replace the fresh green lift but lacks mint's cooling aroma.

key_compounds.name: Carvone
key_compounds.role: A commonly reported spearmint-oil constituent associated with its sweet, green mint aroma; no ingredient-specific local record was available.

key_compounds.name: Limonene
key_compounds.role: A terpene reported in spearmint oils that can contribute citrus-like freshness; composition varies by sample.

key_compounds.name: 1,8-Cineole
key_compounds.role: A reported minor volatile in some spearmint oils, contributing cool herbal notes; not a local measurement.

Curry Leaf.name: Curry Leaf
Curry Leaf.description: Fresh curry leaves are citrusy, leafy, and warm with a distinct, lightly resinous aroma that survives a brief sizzle in oil. They are leaves of Murraya koenigii, not the unrelated dried herb sold as curry plant.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 8-15 leaves per 4 servings, briefly fried in oil

top_pairings.note: A sputtering mustard-seed tempering carries the leaf aroma through oil.
Toasty cumin reinforces the warm, savory base of a tempering.
Earthy turmeric provides a familiar foundation for curry-leaf aromatics.
Chili heat makes the leaves' citrusy fragrance more vivid.
Coriander's citrus-peel quality echoes the leaf's bright top notes.
A small bitter-sweet fenugreek note deepens lentil and vegetable dishes.

substitutes.notes: Adds aromatic depth but misses curry leaf's citrusy, leafy signature.
Can contribute a bright citrus-herbal note, but has a more lemon-forward profile.
Supplies fresh leafy character, but is sweeter and less resinous.

key_compounds.name: α-Pinene
key_compounds.role: A major constituent reported in one analyzed curry-leaf essential oil; its proportion varies by sample and is not a universal value.

key_compounds.name: Sabinene
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile constituent associated with the leaf's fresh, peppery-terpenic aroma.

key_compounds.name: β-Caryophyllene
key_compounds.role: A reported sesquiterpene in curry-leaf oil that can contribute woody, spicy depth.

compound_sources: At authorship, no ingredient-specific local USDA/FooDB/FlavorDB2 record had been inspected; literature compound associations were used. FlavorDB2 evidence was subsequently verified separately; axes remain authored estimates.

Asafoetida.name: Asafoetida
Asafoetida.origin: Iran and Afghanistan; used widely across South Asia
Asafoetida.description: This dried oleo-gum-resin smells forcefully sulfurous raw, then mellows when briefly bloomed in fat into an onion-garlic-like savory note. A pinch seasons lentils, vegetables, and pickles; commercial powders are often diluted with flour.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1/16-1/8 tsp per 4 servings, bloomed in fat
A pinch per 4 servings as an allium-like seasoning

top_pairings.note: Cumin and hing form a savory aromatic base for lentils and vegetables.
Mustard's toasted pungency complements the sulfurous allium-like note.
Earthy turmeric rounds the sharp aroma in dal and vegetable dishes.
Chili brings heat while asafoetida supplies deep savory aroma.
Coriander's citrusy warmth softens the resinous edge.
Fenugreek adds bittersweet depth to the same legumes and vegetables.

substitutes.notes: Closest convenient sulfurous substitute, but lacks asafoetida's resinous aroma.
Provides allium-like savoriness without the same sharp resin note.
Provides a mild fresh allium note without asafoetida's resinous pungency.

key_compounds.name: 2-Butyl 1-propenyl disulfide
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile sulfur compound associated with asafoetida's characteristic pungent aroma.

key_compounds.name: Dimethyl trisulfide
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile sulfur compound contributing the intense sulfurous raw-resin character.

key_compounds.name: Ferulic acid
key_compounds.role: A reported resin constituent; it is part of the nonvolatile resin fraction rather than a measure of the cooked aroma.

key_compounds.name: Umbelliferone
key_compounds.role: A coumarin reported in asafoetida resin; included as a documented phytochemical, not a sensory-intensity claim.

Ajwain.name: Ajwain
Ajwain.origin: Eastern Mediterranean to South Asia; widely cultivated in India
Ajwain.description: Ajwain fruits (often called seeds in kitchens) have a forceful thyme-like, bitter, and warm aroma with a lingering savory edge. Toast or fry briefly and use sparingly in breads, legumes, and fried snacks.

top_pairings.note: Cumin's earthy warmth makes ajwain easier to integrate in doughs and legumes.
Coriander adds citrusy sweetness to ajwain's thyme-like pungency.
Turmeric gives savory vegetables a mellow base for the sharp seed aroma.
A little chili emphasizes ajwain's savory, warming side.
Fenugreek's bitter-sweet quality pairs well in flatbreads and legumes.
Pepper reinforces the pungency while adding a cleaner lingering heat.

substitutes.notes: Echoes the thymol-rich herbal character but is less pungent and less bitter.
Adds warm seed savoriness but lacks ajwain's medicinal thyme-like aroma.
Offers aromatic seed warmth, though its anise-like profile is distinct.

key_compounds.name: Thymol
key_compounds.role: Frequently reported as a major constituent of ajwain fruit essential oil; proportions vary across origins and samples.

key_compounds.name: p-Cymene
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile in ajwain oil, contributing warm, terpene-like aromatic background.

key_compounds.name: γ-Terpinene
key_compounds.role: A reported monoterpene in ajwain oil that contributes fresh, herbal-citrus notes.

key_compounds.name: Carvacrol
key_compounds.role: A reported minor volatile in ajwain oil associated with pungent herbal character.

compound_sources: At authorship, no ingredient-specific local USDA/FooDB/FlavorDB2 record had been inspected; literature compound associations were used. FlavorDB2 evidence was subsequently verified separately; axes remain authored estimates.

Black Cardamom.name: Black Cardamom
Black Cardamom.origin: Eastern Himalaya, especially Nepal, Sikkim, and Bhutan
Black Cardamom.description: Large, smoky-dried pods carry camphoraceous, resinous, and earthy warmth, with a distinctly savory edge. Use whole pods to perfume long-cooked rice, broths, and braises, then remove them before serving.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1 pod per 4 servings in slow-cooked dishes

top_pairings.note: Cumin adds earthy continuity to black cardamom's smoky base.
Coriander lifts the resinous depth with a lighter citrus-seed note.
Clove's sweet pungency fits the same slow-cooked aromatic mixtures.
Cinnamon bridges smoky warmth and the sweetness of rice or braises.
Bay contributes leafy herbal depth to stocks and long-cooked dishes.
Pepper sharpens the heavy, resinous aroma with clean heat.

substitutes.notes: Shares cardamom-family aromatics but is sweeter, brighter, and lacks smoke.
Can provide warm depth, though its clove-cinnamon profile is sweeter.
Contributes pungent depth but not the camphoraceous smoky character.

key_compounds.name: 1,8-Cineole
key_compounds.role: Often reported as a major black-cardamom-oil constituent, associated with its penetrating camphoraceous aroma; abundance varies by sample.

key_compounds.name: α-Terpinyl acetate
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile contributing aromatic, lightly sweet-spicy notes.

key_compounds.name: Sabinene
key_compounds.role: A reported monoterpene contributing fresh, peppery, woody facets.

key_compounds.name: Nerolidol
key_compounds.role: A reported sesquiterpene alcohol that can contribute woody, floral aroma.

compound_sources: No ingredient-specific USDA, FooDB, or FlavorDB2 cache record in local project data; cited samples are not local measurements and composition varies.

Cardamom phytochemical review: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9562589/

Annatto.name: Annatto
Annatto.description: Annatto seeds are valued chiefly for their vivid orange-red color and mild, earthy, peppery aroma. Infuse whole seeds in warm oil or fat and strain; the colorant's flavor is subtle, while over-toasting can turn it bitter.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1-2 tsp seeds infused in oil per 4 servings
1-2 tsp seeds or annatto oil per 4 servings
1-2 tsp annatto seeds infused in oil per 4 servings

top_pairings.note: Cumin adds earthy depth to annatto's gentle peppery base.
Coriander adds citrusy warmth to the mild seed flavor.
Oregano gives annatto-seasoned marinades a savory herbal counterpoint.
Garlic supplies savory depth while annatto colors the oil or paste.
Pepper contributes a lingering bite to annatto's mild earthiness.
Allspice adds sweet warm complexity in Caribbean-style seasoning.

substitutes.notes: Adds red-orange color and mild pepper flavor but not annatto's characteristic pigment.
Provides color and savory warmth, with a much stronger smoky flavor.
Can color oil golden but tastes earthier and yellower.

key_compounds.name: Bixin
key_compounds.role: The principal fat-soluble carotenoid pigment in annatto seed coatings; chiefly responsible for orange-red color, not a claim about measured flavor.

key_compounds.name: Norbixin
key_compounds.role: A water-soluble carotenoid pigment derived from bixin and used in annatto color preparations.

key_compounds.name: Geranylgeraniol
key_compounds.role: A reported isoprenoid constituent of Bixa orellana; included as phytochemical context rather than a dominant seed aroma claim.

compound_sources: No ingredient-specific USDA, FooDB, or FlavorDB2 cache record in local project data; no measured concentrations are asserted.

Epazote.name: Epazote
Epazote.origin: Mexico and Central America; naturalized widely
Epazote.description: Epazote has a pungent, resinous, green aroma with citrus and medicinal facets; use the leaves sparingly, especially dried. It is a traditional seasoning for beans and quesadillas in Mexican cooking.

top_pairings.note: Cumin complements the herb's resinous savoriness in beans.
Oregano brings a familiar savory herbal note alongside epazote's sharper edge.
Coriander contributes citrusy warmth that lifts the pungent green aroma.
Chili heat suits epazote's assertive character in beans and stews.
Pepper adds clean warmth without masking the resinous herb.
Garlic anchors epazote in savory bean and vegetable preparations.

substitutes.notes: Provides savory herbal flavor but lacks epazote's pungent, resinous character.
Adds assertive herbal complexity, though its anise note is different.
Offers pungent green herb notes without epazote's resinous profile.

key_compounds.name: Ascaridole
key_compounds.role: A volatile reported in epazote oil, sometimes abundant; included as a literature association, with no concentration or safety inference for culinary use.

key_compounds.name: p-Cymene
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile in some epazote oils, contributing warm, terpene-like aromatic background.

key_compounds.name: α-Terpinene
key_compounds.role: A reported monoterpene in epazote oil contributing fresh, herbal-citrus character.

key_compounds.name: Carvacrol
key_compounds.role: Reported in some epazote oil profiles and associated with pungent herbal notes; abundance varies.

Huacatay.name: Huacatay
Huacatay.origin: Andean South America, especially Peru and Bolivia
Huacatay.description: Huacatay is the aromatic herb Tagetes minuta, also called Peruvian black mint, and is unrelated to true mint. Its pungent green aroma mixes minty, citrus, and tarragon-like facets; fresh leaves are especially distinctive in Peruvian sauces and stews.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1/4-1 cup chopped fresh leaves per 4 servings
2-4 tbsp fresh leaves or paste per 4 servings

top_pairings.note: Cumin grounds huacatay's vivid herbal aroma in sauces and meat marinades.
Coriander's citrus seed note connects with huacatay's bright top notes.
Aji heat gives huacatay's minty-herbal aroma a savory framework.
Garlic rounds the herb's sharp green character in blended sauces.
Pepper supports the herb's assertive, resinous side.
Oregano adds a familiar savory herb note to the distinctive huacatay aroma.

substitutes.notes: Can imitate a fresh minty lift but lacks huacatay's Tagetes pungency and citrus-tarragon depth.
Adds assertive green, slightly anise-like notes without huacatay's minty citrus quality.
Provides savory herbal backbone but is less bright and distinctive.

key_compounds.name: (Z)-β-Ocimene
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile in Tagetes minuta oil contributing fresh, green aromatic facets; oil composition varies by origin and plant part.

key_compounds.name: (Z)-Tagetone
key_compounds.role: A reported characteristic Tagetes minuta oil constituent associated with its pungent herbal fragrance.

key_compounds.name: Dihydrotagetone
key_compounds.role: A reported major volatile in some T. minuta oils, contributing herbaceous aromatic character.

key_compounds.name: (E)-Tagetenone
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile constituent in T. minuta essential oil; no local concentration is available.

Ají Amarillo.name: Ají Amarillo
Ají Amarillo.origin: Peru and the Andean region of South America
Ají Amarillo.description: Peruvian ají amarillo is a fleshy golden-orange Capsicum baccatum chile with fruity, citrusy flavor and noticeable but rounded heat. Fresh, frozen, paste, and dried mirasol forms differ in brightness and intensity; it is a defining Peruvian seasoning rather than a generic yellow pepper.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1-2 fresh chiles or 1-2 tbsp paste per 4 servings
1-2 chiles or 1-2 tbsp paste per 4 servings

top_pairings.note: Cumin adds earthy warmth to the chile's fruity citrus profile.
Coriander reinforces the bright, citrusy side of ají amarillo.
Garlic provides a savory backbone for sauces and stews.
Pepper adds dry warmth alongside the chile's direct capsaicin heat.
Oregano gives the fruity chile a savory herbal counterpoint.
A small amount complements yellow sauces with earthy color and warmth.

substitutes.notes: Provides heat but is much less fruity and less citrusy; use less.
Offers mild fruity chile flavor, but less brightness and usually less heat.
Adds fruity warmth and color but has a different dried-chile profile.

key_compounds.name: Capsaicin
key_compounds.role: A pungency compound found in Capsicum fruit; amount varies strongly by cultivar, growing conditions, and preparation.

key_compounds.name: Dihydrocapsaicin
key_compounds.role: A pungent capsaicinoid commonly found with capsaicin in chile fruits; not measured for this profile.

key_compounds.name: β-Carotene
key_compounds.role: A carotenoid pigment associated with orange-red Capsicum fruit color; profile does not assert a cultivar-specific amount.

Ají Panca.name: Ají Panca
Ají Panca.description: Ají panca is a Peruvian chile most often used dried or as a paste, with a deep burgundy color, mild-to-moderate heat, and raisiny, smoky-fruity flavor. Taxonomic attributions for panca vary across sources; this profile follows Peruvian native-ají cataloguing that identifies it as Capsicum chinense.

top_pairings.note: Cumin reinforces the earthy bass notes of dried panca chile.
Garlic joins panca in robust marinades, sauces, and braises.
Oregano supplies a savory herbal note that balances dried-fruit sweetness.
Pepper sharpens panca's mellow warmth without obscuring its fruitiness.
Coriander adds a light citrus-seed note to the deep chile flavor.
Paprika supports the red fruit and color while panca contributes deeper dried-chile flavor.

substitutes.notes: Closest broad substitute for mild dried-fruit sweetness, though panca is more distinctive and less raisiny.
Provides dark, fruity dried-chile depth with a different earthy profile.
Adds red color and smoke but lacks panca's chile-fruit flavor.

key_compounds.name: Capsaicin
key_compounds.role: A pungency compound in Capsicum fruits; panca heat depends on cultivar and preparation and is not quantified here.

key_compounds.name: Dihydrocapsaicin
key_compounds.role: A capsaicinoid typically reported alongside capsaicin in chiles; not measured in this profile.

key_compounds.name: β-Carotene
key_compounds.role: A carotenoid associated with red-orange Capsicum pigments; cultivar-specific levels are not asserted.

Rocoto.name: Rocoto
Rocoto.origin: Andean South America, especially Peru and Bolivia
Rocoto.description: Rocoto is the thick-fleshed, distinctly hot Andean chile Capsicum pubescens, often recognized by its dark seeds. It has juicy, fruity flavor and substantial lingering heat; it appears fresh in sauces, relishes, and stuffed preparations.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1/2-1 fresh chile per 4 servings, adjusted for heat

top_pairings.note: Coriander brightens the juicy chile in fresh sauces and relishes.
Earthy cumin supports rocoto in cooked sauces and fillings.
Garlic rounds the fruitiness in rocoto sauces.
Pepper adds a dry second layer of warmth to the chile's direct heat.
Oregano gives fresh rocoto a savory herbal edge.
A small amount can reinforce heat when rocoto is used for fruity aroma rather than full pungency.

substitutes.notes: Matches substantial heat but lacks rocoto's juicy fruit character.
Provides fruity high heat but has a more tropical, floral aroma.
Offers fruity heat, though it is not an Andean pepper and has a distinct aroma.

key_compounds.name: Capsaicin
key_compounds.role: A pungency compound in Capsicum fruit; cultivar and preparation cause large variation, so no measured level is claimed.

key_compounds.name: Dihydrocapsaicin
key_compounds.role: A capsaicinoid commonly present in hot Capsicum fruit; not measured for this profile.

key_compounds.name: β-Carotene
key_compounds.role: A carotenoid pigment found in many Capsicum fruits; included as genus-level context, not a rocoto-specific assay.

Juniper Berry.name: Juniper Berry
Juniper Berry.origin: Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, northern Asia, and North America
Juniper Berry.description: The berry-like cones of common juniper taste resinous, piney, peppery, and faintly citrusy, with a bitter finish if used heavily. Crush lightly and use in moderation with game, cabbage, marinades, or brines.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 3-6 berries per 4 servings in braises or brines

top_pairings.note: Pepper brings a dry bite that complements juniper's piney resin.
Bay adds a leafy woodsy note for brines, game, and braises.
Rosemary echoes the coniferous aroma while adding a savory herbal note.
Caraway's warm seed aroma pairs naturally with cabbage and cured meats.
Thyme softens juniper's resinous edge with a familiar savory herb note.
Allspice contributes warm clove-like sweetness to juniper-seasoned braises.

key_compounds.name: Sabinene
key_compounds.role: A reported juniper-oil monoterpene contributing woody, peppery facets.

key_compounds.name: Myrcene
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile in juniper berry oil contributing green, balsamic aroma.

key_compounds.name: Limonene
key_compounds.role: A reported terpene contributing citrus-like brightness in some juniper oils.

Savory.name: Savory
Savory.origin: Southeastern Europe to western Asia; cultivated widely
Savory.description: This profile means summer savory (Satureja hortensis), an assertive green herb with peppery, thyme-like warmth and a faintly bitter finish. Fresh or dried leaves season beans, vegetables, poultry, and sausages; winter savory is a separate related species.

cuisines.typical_quantity: 1-2 tsp dried or 1-2 tbsp fresh per 4 servings
1 tsp dried or 1 tbsp fresh per 4 servings

top_pairings.note: Thyme shares savory herbal notes while keeping summer savory's peppery edge in balance.
Rosemary adds piney depth to savory's green, peppery character.
Pepper reinforces the herb's warming, piquant impression.
Bay creates a rounded herbal base for beans and braises.
Coriander adds a mild citrus lift to summer savory's pungency.
A little cumin deepens savory bean dishes with an earthy seed note.

substitutes.notes: Closest common substitute, though less peppery and somewhat sweeter.
Provides pungent herbal flavor but has a more floral, Mediterranean profile.
Offers gentle savory herb notes but is milder and sweeter.

key_compounds.name: Thymol
key_compounds.role: A reported volatile in summer savory contributing thyme-like pungency; not a local measurement.

key_compounds.name: γ-Terpinene
key_compounds.role: A reported monoterpene in savory essential oil contributing fresh, herbal-citrus facets.

key_compounds.name: Rosmarinic acid
key_compounds.role: A reported phenolic acid in summer savory extracts; included as phytochemical context, not a volatile aroma measurement.
